name: Mendel's Pea Experiments
statement: By breeding pea plants and counting their traits, Mendel uncovered the hidden rules by which inheritance works.
statementAccent: uncovered the hidden rules by which inheritance works
meaning: Mendel's pea experiments were a series of plant-breeding experiments conducted by Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar at the monastery in Brno, between about 1856 and 1863, which revealed the basic laws of heredity and founded the science of genetics. Working with the common garden pea, Mendel studied seven clearly contrasting traits, such as round versus wrinkled seeds, yellow versus green seeds, and tall versus short plants, crossing true-breeding varieties and carefully counting the offspring over generations. He found that when he crossed two pure lines differing in a trait, the first generation all showed one form, the dominant one, while the other, recessive form vanished, only to reappear in about a quarter of the second generation, giving a characteristic three-to-one ratio. From these results he inferred that each plant carries two hereditary factors, now called alleles, for each trait, one from each parent, and that these separate when gametes form. He also found that different traits are passed on independently of one another. Mendel presented his work in 1865 and published it in 1866, but it was largely ignored until it was rediscovered around 1900, after which it became the foundation of modern genetics.
mechanism: Mendel's method combined careful breeding with quantitative counting. He first established true-breeding lines, plants that reliably produced offspring identical to themselves for a given trait, and then made controlled crosses by transferring pollen between plants differing in a single trait. Crossing a round-seeded with a wrinkled-seeded line, for example, he found that the first generation, the F1, were all round: one form, the dominant, masked the other, the recessive. When he let the F1 self-pollinate, the recessive wrinkled form reappeared in the second generation, the F2, in a ratio of about three dominant to one recessive. Mendel explained this by proposing that each plant carries two hereditary factors for each trait, one inherited from each parent, and that these factors separate during the formation of gametes so that each gamete carries only one, his law of segregation. A plant showing the dominant trait might carry one or two dominant factors, while only plants with two recessive factors show the recessive trait, which produces the three-to-one ratio. By following two traits at once, he further found that they were inherited independently, his law of independent assortment. The consistent numerical ratios revealed the particulate, rule-governed nature of inheritance beneath the visible traits.

examples.text: Crossing round-seeded and wrinkled-seeded pure lines gave all round offspring, with wrinkled reappearing in about a quarter of the next generation.
In the second generation the dominant and recessive forms of a trait appeared in a ratio of about three to one, revealing the hidden factors.
Mendel studied seven contrasting traits, including seed shape and colour, flower colour, pod shape, and plant height.

variants.name: The law of segregation
variants.text: Each plant carries two factors for a trait, which separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries just one.

variants.name: The law of independent assortment
variants.text: Different traits are inherited independently of one another, at least when their genes lie on different chromosomes.

whyItMatters: Mendel's pea experiments are the foundation of genetics, the first work to reveal that inheritance follows precise, discoverable laws rather than a vague blending of parental characters. By showing that traits are passed on as discrete factors, now called genes, that come in pairs, separate into gametes, and combine anew in offspring in predictable ratios, Mendel replaced the old idea that offspring are simply a blend of their parents with a particulate theory of heredity that explains how recessive traits can disappear and reappear across generations. His laws of segregation and independent assortment remain central to genetics, breeding, and medicine, underlying everything from predicting the inheritance of genetic diseases to improving crops and livestock. His careful quantitative method, counting thousands of plants and analyzing ratios, was itself a model of experimental science. Though ignored in his lifetime and rediscovered only around 1900, Mendel's work became the cornerstone on which twentieth-century genetics and the modern understanding of DNA and heredity were built.

working.text: establish pure-breeding pea varieties that reliably pass on a given trait.
cross lines differing in a trait and count the offspring over generations, finding dominant and recessive forms in fixed ratios.
from the three-to-one ratio deduce that paired hereditary factors segregate into gametes and assort independently.

limits: Mendel's laws are foundational but hold under conditions he happened to meet. His law of independent assortment applies only to genes on different chromosomes; genes that lie close together on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, a complication discovered later, and Mendel's seven traits fortunately did not show strong linkage that would have obscured his ratios. Many traits also do not show the simple dominant-recessive pattern of his peas, being shaped by multiple genes, incomplete dominance, or the environment. A genuine historical controversy should be flagged: the statistician R. A. Fisher argued in 1936 that Mendel's data fit the expected ratios suspiciously closely, raising the possibility of unconscious bias in how results were recorded; this remains debated and is not established as fraud. His work was also overlooked for decades before its rediscovery around 1900.
misreadings: Mendel's law of independent assortment is not universal; genes on the same chromosome are linked and do not assort independently, so his laws hold cleanly only for the traits and conditions he studied. His dominant-recessive ratios do not describe all traits, many of which involve several genes or the environment. And the closeness of his data to the expected ratios has been questioned by Fisher as possibly too good, a debate not settled as fraud, so treating independent assortment as always holding, all inheritance as simple dominance, or his data as beyond question, misreads the founding experiments of genetics.
origin: A series of plant-breeding experiments by Gregor Mendel at the monastery in Brno between about 1856 and 1863, presented in 1865 and published in 1866, establishing the laws of inheritance and founding genetics after their rediscovery around 1900.
